column7: The behavioural half of project-row-lock-unscoped-001: replica A holds the project row with the same unscoped FOR UPDATE the fix added, and replica B's DeleteProject cascade must not complete until it is released. Asserts the MECHANISM (mutual exclusion on the project row) rather than the forbidden end state, and that choice is deliberate and load-bearing. An end-state test was written -- 14 iterations racing RestoreProject against DeleteProject, asserting "never (project deleted AND live children)" -- and DELETED after the red proof showed it never reproduced the orphan state even with the fix reverted: it failed only on its own non-vacuity floor, i.e. it reported that the scenario had not occurred. Unsynchronized goroutines do not hit a window this narrow. A deterministic version is impossible by construction rather than merely hard: the interleaving needs the restore to COMMIT between the cascade's child sweeps and its final project UPDATE, which a one-shot GORM-callback hook can arrange only for the BROKEN code -- after the fix the cascade holds the project row from its first statement, so a hooked restore blocks inside the cascade's own callback and the test hangs instead of passing. Shipping the end-state test would have read as coverage of exactly the thing it never exercised. Red-proven: with the pre-fix shape restored on both sides (scoped cascade lock, unlocked restore read) this test fails with "DeleteProject's cascade completed while another replica held the project row", err=project not found. Its held transaction is released through t.Cleanup, not only on the happy path, after an equivalent leak in the break-glass lock-wait test hung a parallel test for a full 600s timeout instead of failing
